title: Everything I Really Need to Know, I Learned in Narnia
author: Mandi Gerth
summary: Mandi Gerth, a classical educator and author, reviews Joshua Herring's Sons of Adam, Daughters of Eve, a study of masculinity and femininity in C.S. Lewis. She came to it doubly sceptical, wondering whether another Lewis book was needed and whether a male author could speak compellingly to women amid a gender crisis, and she ends deeply impressed. Her argument is that Herring shows Lewis recovering what it means to be male and female through the re-enchantment of the imagination, which matches the classical movement's conviction that stories shape how students see the world. She advises teachers to skip to Chapter Four, where Herring catalogues positive and negative images of masculinity and femininity across the Narnia books, including the idea that rightful authority submits to higher authority. Her practical conclusion is that the book models how to read literature wholeheartedly and receptively, a skill many classical teachers lack.
points: Herring argues that recovering what it means to be male and female requires changing the myths people believe, which is work for the imagination as well as for argument.
Classical teachers can use the Narnia chapter of the book as a model for reading stories for their deeper meaning and imagery.
Chapter Four is the practical heart of the book for teachers, cataloguing positive and negative masculine and feminine images in each Narnia story.
The book teaches the Lewisian habit of reading wholeheartedly and receptively, which many classical teachers struggle to model.
quotes: Herring’s book articulately and winsomely persuades that Lewis offers a “recovery of what it means to be male and female” through a re-enchantment of the imagination.
Classical education labors to recover cultural and moral norms that include far more than gender roles, and we have come to believe strongly in the role of story in this recovery.
The stories we share with our students shape and form the way they see the world and their place in it.

Decide whether you want to traverse the winding road into medieval scholarship and modern gender theory that comprises the first half of Sons of Adam, Daughters of Eve or take the express lane straight to Chapter Four
Receiving authority, submitting oneself to the source of that authority, and exercising authority for service of others each contribute to defining the masculine ideal

While most grammar school teachers in a classical school have at least one Narnia book assigned in their literature curriculum, most did not read literature in college the way literature in a classical school needs to be taught.
In my experience, as I have observed classical teachers and conducted hours of teacher training, most teachers struggle to read this way—as one who receives the images as the author intended.
